summary.case_overview: This judgment of a 9-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 494 of 2012 addresses whether the right to privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right under the Constitution of India [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 378]. The reference arose out of a constitutional challenge to the Government of India's Aadhaar scheme, which collects demographic and biometric data, where the State argued that privacy was not a fundamental right based on earlier decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh [Page 15] [Page 282] [Page 308]. The Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms protected under Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431]. In doing so, the Court expressly overruled M.P. Sharma and the portion of Kharak Singh which held that privacy was not protected by the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 352] [Page 430] [Page 431].
summary.facts_of_case: The Government of India propounded a scheme popularly known as the Aadhaar card scheme, under which it collects and compiles demographic and biometric data of residents to be used for various governmental benefits and purposes [Page 15] [Page 308]. A challenge was brought before the Supreme Court asserting that the collection and compilation of such personal data violates the fundamental 'Right to Privacy' [Page 15]. During the proceedings, the Union Government contested the existence of a fundamental right to privacy, relying on the decisions of an 8-Judge Bench in M.P. Sharma and a 6-Judge Bench in Kharak Singh [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 282] [Page 378]. To resolve the conflict in judicial precedent and interpret substantial questions of constitutional law, a reference was made pursuant to Article 145(3) to a 9-Judge Constitution Bench [Page 11] [Page 15] [Page 378]. The 9-Judge Bench clarified that it was constituted solely to decide the threshold constitutional question of whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right, and not to determine the ultimate constitutional validity of the Aadhaar Act itself, which was sent back for adjudication on merits by a 3-Judge Bench [Page 5] [Page 308] [Page 352] [Page 431].

summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners contended that privacy is a natural, primordial, and inalienable right inherent in human existence and inseparable from human dignity and personal liberty [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 4] [Page 9] [Page 378] [Page 405]. They submitted that modern technology allows non-state and state entities to intrude into a citizen's private life without physical entry, necessitating constitutional recognition of privacy across Part III rights [Page 10] [Page 62] [Page 428]. The Attorney General for India argued on behalf of the Union that the Constitution does not guarantee a fundamental right to privacy, as the framers consciously omitted a provision similar to the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution [Page 282] [Page 378]. The Attorney General further submitted that the right to life has primacy over personal liberty, and in a developing country where millions lack basic necessities like food, shelter, and jobs, claims to privacy cannot override state welfare delivery schemes like Aadhaar [Page 308]. Counsel for the State of Gujarat (Rakesh Dwivedi) argued for an intermediate approach, contending that privacy claims should be recognized only when a person satisfies the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test, and that voluntarily parting with personal data to avail benefits diminishes that expectation [Page 282].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court reasoned that fundamental rights, including privacy, are natural and inalienable human rights that inhere in individuals by virtue of being human, rather than bounties conferred by the State or created by the constitutional document [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 9] [Page 15] [Page 19] [Page 308] [Page 352]. Re-evaluating precedent, the Court noted that M.P. In Kharak Singh, while night domiciliary visits were rightly held to violate ordered liberty, the second part declaring privacy not to be a guaranteed right was unreasoned and erroneous [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 5] [Page 6]. The Court explained that privacy is intrinsically linked to individual dignity, autonomy, and liberty, serving as a functional condition precedent for exercising freedoms across Part III, including Articles 14, 19, 20(3), 21, 25, 28, and 29 [Page 2] [Page 5] [Page 6] [Page 7] [Page 54] [Page 150] [Page 264] [Page 387]. Rejecting an originalist interpretation, the Court affirmed that the Constitution is a sacred living document that evolves to meet technological developments and digital footprints [Page 11] [Page 12] [Page 27] [Page 62] [Page 413] [Page 417].
